Gualeguaychú is a city in the Entre Ríos Province in Argentina. It is on the left bank of the Gualeguaychú River, a tributary of the Uruguay River. In 2010, 109,266 people lived there. The city hosts an carnival Corsódromo de Gualeguaychú, which is held every year on Saturdays of January and February. It is thought to be one of the largest carnivals in the world. Gualeguaychú also has hot springs, beach resorts, and a casino. Gualeguaychú is not be confused with Gualeguay, another city also in Entre Ríos, about 80 km (50 mi) west. Gualeguaychú was founded on October 18, 1783 by Tomas de Rocamora.

Guantánamo Province is the easternmost province of Cuba. Its capital is the city of Guantánamo, which functions as the main administrative and economic center of the province. The region is geographically distinct within Cuba, bordered by the Caribbean Sea to the south and the Windward Passage to the east, across from Haiti. It also includes varied landscapes such as coastal plains, mountain ranges like the eastern end of the Sierra Maestra, and some of the island’s most isolated rural and natural areas. Guantánamo Province has an economy that is largely based on agriculture, livestock, and local services, with sugarcane, coffee, and cocoa historically being important crops in different parts of the province. The coastal municipality of Baracoa, one of the oldest European settlements in Cuba, is also part of the province and is known for its cultural heritage and natural surroundings. In addition to agriculture and small-scale industry, the province has developed some tourism activity, especially in areas with beaches, mountains, and ecological reserves. One of the most internationally recognized features associated with the province is the presence of the Guantanamo Bay Naval Base, a U.S. naval installation located on the southeastern coast of the province. It has a distinct legal and political status and is separated from the Cuban-administered territory of the province. Administratively, Guantánamo Province was established in its current form in 1976, when Cuba reorganized its national territorial divisions. Prior to this reform, the area was part of the larger historic province of Oriente, which covered much of eastern Cuba. The division of Oriente into several smaller provinces, including Guantánamo, was intended to create more localized administrative regions. Today, Guantánamo remains one of Cuba’s more geographically remote provinces, with a combination of coastal communities, mountainous interior regions, and agricultural zones. While it is less urbanized than western provinces like Havana, it maintains a distinct regional identity shaped by its geography, history, and cultural heritage.

Guantánamo Bay is a bay in Guantánamo province, Cuba. It is at the southeastern end of Cuba. It is the largest harbour on the south side of the island. It is surrounded by steep hills creating an enclave cut off from its immediate hinterland. The bay was originally named Guantánamo by the Taíno. Christopher Columbus landed at the location known as Fisherman's Point in 1494, naming it Puerto Grande. On landing, Columbus's crew found Taíno fisherman preparing a feast for the local chieftain. When Spanish settlers took control of the island, the bay became a vital harbor on the south side of the island. The bay has been the focus of military activities for a long time. In the colonial era, British troops tried to land there during the War of the Jenkin's Ear. That war was between England and Spain and lasted from 1739 to 1742. The troops could land in the bay, and later tried to take the city Santiago de Cuba. As it turned out, this was impossible. So the troops claimed the bay as theirs, and named it Cumberland Harbour. Later they left the island again, because some of their troops had died from tropical diseases. The United States tried to buy the whole island of Cuba. In the Spanish-American war, US troops occupied the bay, because there was a harbour there. The Treaty of Paris, between the United States and Spain ended the war. This treaty gave Cuba its independence from Spain. Spain also gave the territory of Puerto Rico and the islands of Guam and the Philippines to the United States, amongst others. Cuba, however, came under the political and military influence of the United States. The US then put presidents and dictators at the head of the Cuban state. These were of course favorable to the interests of the United States. In 1902 the Platt Amendment was appended to the Constitution of the Cuban state. It limited the freedom of Cuba very much. It also said that some territory in the south should be ceded to the United States for a military base. Bound by the amendment, the Cubans granted the US a 99-year lease to the territory. This treaty was made by Tomás Estrada Palma, an American citizen, who became the first President of Cuba. The current Cuban government rejects the Cuban-American Treaty because it violates article 52 of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties. The Cuban government therefore considers the U.S. presence in Guantánamo to be an illegal occupation of the area. Article 52 declares a treaty void only if it was obtained through a threat or use of force in violation of international law. The southern portion of the bay is surrounded by the Guantanamo Bay Naval Base, an American naval base established in 1898. Recently, the base began hosting a detainment camp for suspected militant combatants collected from both Afghanistan and Iraq, or from secret NATO prisons in Europe (discovered in 2006). Some critics view this as kidnapping. The base, sometimes called "GTMO" or "Gitmo", covers 116 km² (about 45 square miles) on the western and eastern banks of the bay. It was established in 1898, when the United States obtained control of Cuba from Spain at the end of the Spanish-American War, following the 1898 invasion of Guantánamo Bay.
